Q: psql select integer in selected arrays A:

The error occurs because a2 is an array column (integer[]), while the IN operator expects a set of scalar values, not arrays.

This subquery:

SELECT a2 FROM t2s WHERE id = #{id}

returns one or more rows, each containing an integer[].
So PostgreSQL ends up trying to compare:

bigint = integer[]

which is not a valid operation.

Even if the subquery returns only one row (using FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY), the result is still a row containing an array, not a list of integers.

To check whether a value exists inside an array, PostgreSQL provides array operators such as ANY.
If you want to use IN, the array must first be expanded into individual rows using unnest().

Using ANY (recommended when the subquery returns one row):

SELECT id
FROM t1s
WHERE x1 = ANY (
    SELECT a2
    FROM t2s
    WHERE id = #{id}
);

Using unnest (when the subquery may return multiple rows):

SELECT id
FROM t1s
WHERE x1 IN (
    SELECT unnest(a2)
    FROM t2s
    WHERE id = #{id}
);

Q: SpringBoot Model Advice A:

If I understood you correct your model is Ok, that is, having a Category with parentId. Now this I did not understand: "Now you cannot save something with the Parent ID, but there are some Categories, that don't have any child categories." The closest thing I can think of is you meant ...without a parent ID... If that is the case this assumption is wrong, you can definitely save something without a parent ID and those can be considered logically and physically (DB) root categories. Having one table imho is better if in future you want sub sub (or n child subs). And assuming you meant "cannot" Why is that? Here is an example already implemented: https://github.com/Damiox/ecommerce-rest-spring-jpa

Q: How can http.Server be made to hold open a connection? A:

There is no simple configuration to change, alas. The trick is to have the request body be slow to read, as described in the third item I (thought) I tried, and for the handler to actually read it. In the updated playground, the code uses a custom io.Reader that is slow to read:

type holdOpen struct{}

func (holdOpen) Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) {
    time.Sleep(time.Second)
    return 0, nil
}

Then, after making the request, wait long enough for it to start to be handled by the server, like so:

req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(t.Context(), http.MethodGet, url, holdOpen{})

go func(req *http.Request) {
    http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
}(req)
time.Sleep(time.Millisecond * 10)

This gives the server long enough to start handling the request, and be waiting on the client to send the body. Then send the signal.

A couple other reasons my original test wasn't working (🤦🏻‍♂️):

  • Making a POST request to a GET handler won't work
  • Making an https to an http server won't work

Q: Keystore location (Linux) A:

You should specify the keystore to which you're saving the key. (See the Oracle documentation.) You could create a new keystore, or use the Java one in [java]/jre/lib/security.

From Oracle:

keytool -genkey -alias keyAlias -keyalg RSA -keypass changeit -storepass changeit -keystore keystore.jks

The default password is "changeit" -- simplest to keep this for development.

As an aside, it's probably best to avoid doing this (or much else) as root anyway. Use sudo if you can.
